confidence_note: The core story (Edmondson expected better hospital teams to make fewer medication errors, found they reported more, and concluded that the difference lay in willingness to report) is consistent across secondary sources and a quoted book excerpt, but I could not read the book's page. Omitted because not verified: the year of the study, the number of units or hospitals, any statistics, how many nurses, the names of units. The later finding that psychologically safe units made fewer errors on more objective data is from a reader's quote of the book and is used only as 'as she reports'.
facts: Early in her research Edmondson studied medication errors in hospital units, expecting that better teams would make fewer errors.
The data pointed the other way: the units with better teamwork and leadership reported more errors.
She concluded the difference was in reporting, not in doing: in some units people felt safe to say that something had gone wrong.
In units where staff feared blame, errors were hidden, so nobody could learn from them.
She came to call this shared belief that you will not be punished for speaking up psychological safety.
She reports that when she looked at more objective, independent measures of errors, the psychologically safe units did not make more errors; the higher the safety, the fewer errors.
The apparent paradox was a measurement problem: a low count of reported errors can mean a team is hiding them.
scene_details: a hospital unit's medication error reports
units where staff feared retribution for reporting
an expected result that came out reversed
tension: The teams that looked best on paper reported the most mistakes, the opposite of what she predicted.
opening_idea: Open on the data: the better the team, the longer its list of errors.

lessons.idea: A quiet record of mistakes can mean people are hiding them, so judge a team by how safely problems come up, not by how few it shows.
lessons.anchor: the better hospital teams reported more errors

reflect_final: If someone on your team spotted a small problem today, how would they decide whether to tell you, and what could you do to make telling easier?

use_cases.situation: A team report shows almost no problems.
use_cases.move: Say that Edmondson found the best hospital teams reported the most errors, and ask what people are not telling you.

use_cases.situation: Someone brings you a mistake they made.
use_cases.move: Thank them first and ask what they learned, so the next person sees what telling costs.

use_cases.situation: A child hides a broken thing at home.
use_cases.move: React to the broken object with a calm question about what happened before any blame.

pocket_idea: Edmondson's best hospital units reported more errors, not fewer: a spotless record may only mean people are afraid to speak.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Edmondson expected the best hospital teams to make the fewest errors, and found they reported the most.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Amy Edmondson studied medication errors expecting better teams to make fewer. Instead they reported more. The best teams were not making more mistakes: their people felt safe saying something had gone wrong, while in units where staff feared blame the errors stayed hidden.
